Google Workspace now includes a complete set of AI features to help small and micro businesses save time, effort, and money.

For a limited time, 9to5Mac readers can get 20% off any of the Business Starter, Standard, and Plus intends for the first six months ….

Industry observers note that google Workspace is a cloud-based productivity and collaboration suite integrating Google apps, file storage, and content creation tools into a single platform accessible from any device. This now includes Gemini AI features as standard!

Whether you’re a solopreneur or a small business owner, Google Workspace offers enterprise-grade capabilities that include custom email domains, centralized administration, and fully scalable storage and support. Three main tiers are available, with the flexibility to upgrade as your business grows:.

According to recent reports, aims can be purchased as a flexible monthly subscription or annually to save money. There’s also an enterprise tier available for companies that make it into the major league.

Business Starter includes Gemini assistance in Gmail and the standalone Gemini Chat app. In-depth assistance within other Google apps requires Business Standard or higher.

Gemini in Gmail and Google Docs can help you create compelling sales and marketing copy across all channels: brochures, web copy, sales pitches, proposals, blog posts, social media, customer emails, and more.

According to recent reports, gemini can also bring your marketing campaigns to life with eye-catching imagery. A simple prompt is all you need to generate editable slides and visuals.

Gemini takes you from blank page to brilliance by generating fully-formatted first drafts of all your promotional materials without countless hours of work or expensive external consultants.

You can create polished sales and marketing videos in minutes with Google Vids by using Gemini to transform static product images into high-quality animations.

In a recent development, with Gemini Omni included in Google Vids, you can even create videos using your personal avatar. Text-to-speech capabilities provide AI voiceovers and avatar narration with natural-sounding inflections, pacing, and context-aware emphasis.

Gemini can also transform static Google Docs, PDFs, and Word files into engaging video summaries. Gemini generates scripts and narration while providing custom visuals to bring your documents to life.

If you’ve ever wished you had an administrative assistant with you during video calls for sales pitches and client meeting, Gemini in Meet can take notes for you and then automatically generate summaries and action points.

For businesses that work internationally, Gemini in Meet can also break down language barriers, translating speech in real time – with translated captions for 60+ languages. In addition, people who are hearing-impaired or who prefer to follow the conversation in a visual format can turn on live captions.

Gemini can even ensure you look your best in video calls, applying features like studio lighting and AI-generated backgrounds to present a polished and professional image.

Gemini in Sheets can act as a business analyst and researcher, helping you carry out tasks like building cash flow models, creating project schedules, and pulling together competitive research tables.

In a recent development, gemini can identify the external data you need and automatically paste the figures directly into Google Sheets documents. If you want to dig deeper into any of the data, Gemini provides the exact web sources used for each individual cell.

For tasks like summarizing, categorizing, and processing internal business data, Gemini assistance lets you carry out this work up to 55 times faster than manual entry based on a 500-cell task.

You can even create custom mini apps in Sheets just by using simple prompts.

It has been revealed that no business can risk client or internal business data leaking into public AI models. Google Workspace Privacy Hub ensures that all your interactions with Gemini remain completely confidential.

Your content is never used for AI training or subject to human review unless you choose to grant permission.

A single subscription combines the complete Google Workspace productivity suite and Gemini AI capabilities (Gmail and standalone app with Business Starter, the full set of AI tools with all other tiers).

It has been revealed that the discount is valid for the first 6 months of service on eligible Business plans (Starter, Standard, Plus), must be redeemed during initial billing setup, and will be applied at checkout. Full terms and conditions can be found here.

#73864. Industry News: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth

Industry News: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2070 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gpupartner

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen.
  • With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.
  • In a recent development, openAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.

With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.

In a recent development, openAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.

That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.

Industry observers note that since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.

Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).

Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.

Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:.

That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.

Industry observers note that it depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.

On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.

Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.

The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.

Industry observers note that if you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.

For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.

Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.

If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs.

In a recent development, if you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.

RTX 5060 8GB, RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 5070 12GB.

Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE).

RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, RTX 5070 Ti, RTX 5080, RTX PRO 2000.

Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini.

RTX 3090, RTX 4090, RX 7900 XTX, RTX PRO 4000.

RTX 5090 32GB, RTX PRO 4500 32GB, RTX PRO 5000 48GB, RTX PRO 6000 96GB.

RTX 5060 8GB, RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 5070 12GB.

Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE).

RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, RTX 5070 Ti, RTX 5080, RTX PRO 2000.

Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini.

RTX 3090, RTX 4090, RX 7900 XTX, RTX PRO 4000.

RTX 5090 32GB, RTX PRO 4500 32GB, RTX PRO 5000 48GB, RTX PRO 6000 96GB.

Models marked MoE (mixture of experts) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way.

Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate.

Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context.

It has been revealed that nothing else in this guide changes. Revision Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2.

It has been revealed that those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower.

Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station, not a graphics card.

Yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory. Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon.

The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark.

Industry observers note that it takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along.

In a recent development, first, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup.

Recent findings suggest that I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription.

The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor.

Once you've clicked through the installer and introduced Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one.

Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded.

Industry observers note that on the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B.

According to recent reports, the model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list.

Sources indicate that you should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU.

In a recent development, every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting.

Sources indicate that once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need.

I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU.

At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth.

Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup.

Short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network.

According to recent reports, once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC.

Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab.

Settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part.

Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set.

Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it.

Industry observers note that not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network.

If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away.

In the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship.

As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help.

PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to let me know and I'll give them a go!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 22, 2026 at 4:00PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Procter & Gamble ›.

The most interesting thing Procter & Gamble (PG +0.91%) made this year might be a diaper.

According to recent reports, it's called Pampers Amoira, P&G's most premium diaper yet. It was built on a simple insight: Families are having fewer babies, so parents are willing to spend more on each one. CFO Andre Schulten said Amoira is on track to top $100 million in U.S. sales in its first year.

According to recent reports, that one product indicates a lot about where P&G is headed, and it's why I'd want to own the stock before 2027. The 70-year dividend streak is just the bonus.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Recent findings suggest that jejurikar, a P&G lifer who joined in 1989, became CEO on Jan. 1. He isn't tearing up the strategy so much as changing how it's carried out. P&G is spending more time in shoppers' homes, making brand content for algorithm-driven social feeds, and working with retailers on everything from store displays to AI shopping tools.

Recent findings suggest that it's working so far. Organic sales rose 4% last quarter, mostly because people bought more products rather than paid higher prices. "Growth going forward is not about taking share. Growth going forward is about growing our categories," Schulten said.

P&G also bought Thorne, a premium supplements brand. "It's a really well-run operation, and it's been around for a long time," Jejurikar told CNBC.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest reason is a restructuring program that cuts up to 7,000 non-manufacturing jobs and exits some weaker brands and markets over two fiscal years. Schulten called it "an vital step toward ensuring our ability to deliver our long-term algorithm over the coming two to three years." In this year's annual report letter, Jejurikar wrote that P&G is "committed to improving results semester by semester and year by year.".

Sources indicate that the road there runs through higher oil prices, though. "Due to the duration of higher oil prices, we now expect materially higher cost headwinds in Q2 and the second half of fiscal 2027," Schulten warned, and P&G is "closely watching consumer demand as high fuel and energy costs persist into the fall and winter." That's partly why P&G expects core earnings growth of just 0% to 3% this fiscal year, and its pricing power is limited, since price increases had only a minor effect on sales last quarter.

At about 26 times earnings and near its 52-week high, the stock also carries a full P/E ratio for a company growing earnings in the low single digits.

Still, I'd rather own P&G while the hard work is happening than wait until the payoff is obvious. Trusted brands, a leaner cost base, and new products like Amoira are the kind of economic moat that rewards patience. Buying before the savings show up beats paying up once everyone can see them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

Industry observers note that 2027 is going to be a relatively massive iPhone release year for Apple. First, the organization will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a upcoming round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

Recent findings suggest that for the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the latest Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will revision the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 currently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

It has been revealed that this phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

In a recent development, out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too crucial – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

It has been revealed that for the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Sources indicate that personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

Industry observers note that lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-revealed iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

#73860. Industry News: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

Industry News: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • Sources indicate that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Recent findings suggest that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

Sources indicate that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

According to recent reports, amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

It has been revealed that RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The organization’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company declared a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

Sources indicate that but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Industry observers note that such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s key to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Sources indicate that to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

Industry observers note that in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the tech giant’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

It has been revealed that in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

According to recent reports, the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

In a recent development, consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its people because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted prepares for achieving long-term objectives.

It has been revealed that the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Sources indicate that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

Recent findings suggest that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Run macOS userspace on Linux by loading the macOS kernel into it.

xnulinux builds XNU, the open-source kernel of macOS, from Apple's published sources and runs it as a loadable kernel module (xnu.ko) inside an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel. The hosted XNU drives the CPU and MMU directly, so macOS processes run natively next to Linux processes on the same CPUs, with no hypervisor between them. Linux lends XNU its memory, timers, files, network and GPU through a small interface module (fki.ko).

With a stock Ubuntu kernel, insmod xnu.ko boots a macOS 27 system disk made by Apple's own installer to the desktop: loginwindow, WindowServer, Dock, Finder, Safari and Chrome.

It has been revealed that one system, two userspaces. Left: a Terminal in the hosted macOS 27.2.1 (sw_vers, the Darwin kernel, launchd, WindowServer, Dock and Finder running). Right: from that macOS, an SSH session into the Linux it runs inside (Ubuntu, Linux 7.0, the xnu and fki modules loaded, and the insmod xnu.ko process the macOS kernel runs in). Straight from the hosted framebuffer, 1280×800.

The hosted desktop at the end of a 30-minute stress run, rendered on the CPU (no GPU bridge).

Safari in the hosted macOS: Wikipedia's article on XNU, kernel.org and the Linux repository on GitHub, over the hosted system's network link through Linux, with the GPU bridge on (GPU=auto).

Working, on an Apple Silicon Mac running an arm64 Linux VM (krunkit) with 1 to 6 hosted CPUs:.

What is still a stopgap is listed in docs/production.md. Notably: the OS cryptex is merged into the system volume, AMFI is patched and SIP relaxed, and memory access is slower than a native VM (4K pages vs 16K).

In a recent development, the Linux side and the XNU side are kept apart by license and meet only at FKI. Every source file carries an SPDX-License-Identifier; the license texts are in LICENSES/.

xnu.ko is on the XNU side of the line: it runs XNU's code in its own address space, so it is APSL-2.0 like XNU, and Linux reports it as a non-GPL module (MODULE_LICENSE("Proprietary"), which taints the kernel as ZFS does). It must not include Linux headers beyond the module ABI, call Linux functions other than fki_*, or carry Linux code. Upstream code (XNU, macOS-DroidVM's toolchain, Mesa, metal2vulkan, the Vulkan loader, LLVM) is fetched at pinned revisions and patched at build time; it is never committed.

Clinical progress extends into autosomal dominant optic atrophy, an inherited disorder causing vision loss. Phase I dosing for STK-002 tests whether targeting protein deficiency translates into improved sight.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Lawrence Rothman, CFA – Nov 22, 2026 at 4:14PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Altria Group ›.

Industry observers note that altria Group (MO +0.25%) has a remarkable dividend history. It has raised the payment 61 times over the last 57 years. That puts the company firmly among the Dividend Kings — a small group of stocks with active payout-hiking streaks of at least 50 consecutive years.

The company has prioritized dividends, and management targets mid-single-digit percentage increases annually. It met that target this year by raising the quarterly payout by 4.7% to $1.11 per share.

That annualizes to a payout of $4.44 a year, which at Friday's closing share price of $74.87 gives it a dividend yield of 5.9%. For comparison, the S&P 500 index yields 1.1%.

In a recent development, what if you're targeting a specific amount in annual dividends — say, $5,000? To get that, you'd need to purchase 1,126 shares for about $84,300. Of course, that assumes Altria Group's dividends will remain constant, which they haven't, obviously.

But before income investors make a decision about purchasing this high-yielding Dividend King, they should take a deeper look at Altria Group's underlying business fundamentals.

In a recent development, the maker of tobacco and e-vapor products has been watching its product sales volumes decrease for some time. That's particularly true for its core cigarette business, which falls under its smokeable tobacco group.

Industry observers note that in the first nine months of this year, smokeable tobacco products' revenue, excluding excise taxes, increased 3.6% year over year. However, this increase came entirely from the firm increasing the prices it charges. The volume of cigarettes and other smokeables it sold dropped 2.7%, primarily driven by cigarettes' 2.8% volume decline.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Relying on a regular cadence of price increases on smokers to offset volume declines isn't a recipe for long-term success. While Altria management remains committed to paying and raising its dividends, it can't fight weakening business fundamentals forever. While the dividend seems secure for now, the company's relatively high 89% payout ratio suggests that may not be the case forever, unless the business finds other ways to raise its revenues.

That's why I think investors looking for dividends can find better alternatives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of Apple’s most beloved products this year was undoubtedly the MacBook Neo. Unlike some of its other budget products, Apple seems interested in updating the MacBook Neo on an annual cycle, and we may get the next MacBook Neo around March.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, Apple is targeting the iOS/macOS 27.4 release cycle for the release of the new MacBook Neo, as well as the A19 budget iPad, iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and OLED iPad Air.

According to recent reports, while he notes that this cycle runs between February and March, it doesn’t necessarily mean the products will launch on the earlier end of that spectrum. Apple is also expected to release the iPhone Air 2, OLED iPad Air, and a new iPad Pro within the first half of the year, but they’ll likely come a bit later than the aforementioned products.

As expected, the next MacBook Neo will bump up from the A18 Pro chip with 8GB of RAM to the A19 Pro chip with 12GB of RAM.

Apple will also introduce newly introduced colors on the MacBook Neo “frequently,” though it’s unclear if we’ll see that with the next iteration. From the Power On newsletter:.

Industry observers note that the other thing I’ve heard is that Apple looks to refresh the MacBook Neo’s colors frequently. We’ll see if that trend starts with the first follow-up.

In a recent development, I’m certainly excited to see the next generation MacBook Neo, especially with 12GB of unified memory. While 8GB is certainly fine, heavy multitaskers will notice it, especially with unoptimized software.

As a personal trainer, I proposal my sessions the same way every time: a mobility-focused warm-up, the session plan itself, then a cool-down full of deep holds and static stretches.

The idea is to prepare your joints and muscles for movement and encourage blood flow around the body, which you won't really do by folding over your legs to stretch your hamstrings.

Building flexible muscles and mobile joints isn't just about sitting cross-legged or touching your toes; it's about combining strength, balance, control and stability, and increasing range of motion.

Sources indicate that the next time you warm up before a run, try these three dynamic exercises instead. Below, I show you how to do them and why.

Sources indicate that if you experience pain at any time, stop and rest. If you're working with an injury or health condition, or you're currently pregnant or postnatal, I recommend seeking advice before starting these exercises.

Sources indicate that the routine: 50 seconds on, 10 seconds off, 3 rounds. Add or reduce the number of rounds if you prefer.

If you run often or you watch a lot of soccer, you know how nasty a hamstring injury can be, and how long it takes to recover. It can come out of nowhere, too, sending you into a slow, painful hobble. We want to avoid that by warming these tender muscle groups properly before a workout, and to do that, I encourage you to add gentle motion to your warm-ups.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Really, these three moves target more than just your hamstrings, but I highly recommend them as part of a wider routine or as a standalone session. If you have very tight muscles, a soft knee bend will help in downward dog, and during the Cossack squat, reducing your squat depth will be helpful.

Keeping active and moving around often will also move blood around the body, delivering more oxygen to the working muscle groups. Equally, staying on your feet longer means activating your calves, which are known as the second heart, as contracting the calf muscles pumps deoxygenated blood back toward the heart.

In a recent development, the moral of the story? Walk (and practice mobility) before you run.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Hisense 65M7SR probably won't win any spec-sheet battles, but for what it costs, that won't matter. Its Mini-LED picture looked great across every piece of content I threw at it, Roku's interface is a joy to use as always, and it handled casual gaming without a hitch. If you can grab one on sale, it’s an absolute steal.

Vivid, colorful Mini-LED picture for the money.

Dolby Vision support at a budget price.

Slim design that doesn't scream "budget TV".

60Hz panel and HDMI 2.0 ports limit high FPS gaming.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Mini-LED used to be something you paid a premium for. Now, it's showing up on the best TVs that cost less than a weekend trip. The Hisense 65M7SR is a prime example of that: a 65-inch Mini-LED TV with Dolby Vision, Roku's famously streamlined interface, and a list price of $699.99 that I wouldn't expect anyone to actually pay (it’s on sale often for as low as $399.99).

Industry observers note that this is Hisense's entry point into Mini-LED, so it makes a couple of trade-offs to hit that price, namely a 60Hz panel and HDMI 2.0 port setup. I spent some time with the 65-inch model, watching reveals on Netflix, soaking in 4K videos on YouTube, and playing a couple of PlayStation 5 games, and I came away much more impressed than I expected. The 65M7SR won’t dazzle anyone on paper, but in my real-world tests, it held its own very well.

The Hisense 65M7SR debuted in September 2026 and comes in a handful of sizes. Here's how the lineup breaks down:.

• Hisense 50M7SR (50-inch): $499.99.

• Hisense 55M7SR (55-inch): $549.99.

• Hisense 65M7SR (65-inch): $699.99.

• Hisense 75M7SR (75-inch): $899.99.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

• Hisense 85M7SR (85-inch): $1,299.99.

Sources indicate that that $699.99 sticker price is more of a suggestion at this point. I've seen the 65-inch model drop to just $399.99 more than once, and that's the price I’d expect to see it at for some time (still, snag one promptly if you absolutely want to lock in that discount). At $700, there are better TVs out there than the 65M7SR, but at $400, I think the purchase makes a lot more sense.

Dolby Vision, HDR 10, Hybrid Log-Gamma (HLG).

3 x HDMI 2.0, 1 x LAN, 1 x Optical digital audio, 1 x USB-A 2.0.

Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth, Apple AirPlay 2.

56.9 x 34.6 x 11.7 (w/ stand); 56.9 x 33 x 2.6 in (w/o stand).

The 65M7SR sticks to the budget TV design playbook, but it pulls it off with a little more polish than I expected. The bezels are slim, the frame has a simple flat black, and the whole thing measures just 2.6 inches deep, so it won't look bulky on a stand or mounted on the wall. Without the stand, it weighs 38.4 pounds, so moving it around is pretty easy.

The 65M7SR sticks to the budget TV design playbook, but it pulls it off with a little more polish than I expected.

Sources indicate that if you'd rather set it on furniture, the included feet can be placed in two different configurations: sitting out toward the edges of the screen, or closer to the center. I like keeping them at the center because they take up less space and are compatible with more media setups. That’s why center pedestal stands will always be best in my eyes, but this style comes in at a close second. It's a clean, no-frills look, and I mean that as a compliment.

The 65M7SR has three HDMI ports, all of which are HDMI 2.0 (that, coupled with the fact that its refresh rate of 60Hz means is not going to make the list of our best gaming TVs. ). Still, one of them supports eARC, so you can hook up a soundbar without sacrificing an input. Beyond that, you get a USB-A port, Ethernet, optical digital audio out, and a cable/antenna input.

Three HDMI ports are plenty for most setups, though if you've got a soundbar, a console, and a Blu-ray player, you'll fill them up quickly. Another thing to note: the 65M7SR doesn’t support Bluetooth, so you can't pair wireless devices directly with the TV. That's a bummer, but I don’t feel it’s a deal-breaker at this price.

Recent findings suggest that I started my testing with "East of Eden" on Netflix, and the picture looked great right away. Colors were rich, and skin tones looked natural compared to the overcooked look that many budget TVs fall victim to. SDR brightness is a strength here (the 65M7SR hit 466 nits in our testing, the highest in the test results table below), so the image stayed punchy and easy to see even with the lights on. Dolby Vision support (which is rare on a TV at this price) made the whole experience feel more cinematic than I expected.

Sources indicate that next up was "Cyberpunk Edgerunners 2," also on Netflix, and it might have been my favorite stretch of the whole test. The show's neon-soaked city is basically a stress test for color, and the 65M7SR handled it with ease. Signs and lights popped against the dark backdrops, and the fast-moving action scenes stayed crisp and smooth.

Input latency (in milliseconds).

In a recent development, for our technical tests, we use a Jeti spectraval 1501-HiRes spectroradiometer, a Klein K10-A colorimeter, a Murideo 8K-SIX-G Metal pattern generator, and Portrait Displays’ Calman TV calibration software to take measurements. We also use a Leo Bodnar 4K Input Lag Tester for determining whether it’s one of the best gaming TVs.

Subjective tests vary based on the reviewer, but usually feature anecdotes from a diverse selection of movies, TV reveals, and other content reflecting the types of things you may actually want to watch on the TV.

For a more detailed look at what we do and how we do it, check out our “How we test TVs” page.

Industry observers note that netflix’s "Grand Theft Auto VI Extended Look” looked just as good, with sharp detail and plenty of pop. The detail in the sun-bleached streets and the saturated sunsets came through clearly, though this is where the TV highlighted some of its limits. It peaked at just 463 nits in our HDR tests, which is the lowest in our results table, so don't expect searing highlights. I never felt like I was missing out while watching, but a brighter set like the Hisense U6SF Pro will make HDR content look a lot brighter. The TCL QM64L is another strong budget pick for HDR brightness at 630 nits and a great Amazon-Vega-OS-based alternative to the 65M7SR.

In a recent development, I also threw on some 4K nature videos on YouTube to see how the TV handles real-world detail, and they looked great. Foliage, water, and wildlife were richly detailed, and the colors were lively without being overly saturated or cartoonish. Color accuracy isn't the 65M7SR's strongest suit with a Delta-E of 3.05, but I didn't see anything that looked off, and its 95.16% UHDA-P3 coverage gives it plenty of range.

Industry observers note that gaming performance is solid for the price. I played some of "Marvel's Spider-Man 2" and "Marvel's Wolverine" on a PlayStation 5 to test the TV's gaming features, and both looked and felt great. Game Mode Plus and ALLM kept things feeling snappy, and VRR support helped keep the action smooth.

The 65M7SR's 13.8ms input lag is slightly higher than that of the other TVs in the results table, but I couldn't notice it at all. Swinging through Manhattan still looked gorgeous, and Wolverine's fast-paced brawls felt responsive from start to finish. The one catch is that the 60Hz panel and HDMI 2.0 ports mean you won't get the 120Hz modes that some games offer, so if you want that, you'll need to spend more.

Industry observers note that the 65M7SR's built-in speakers are a 20W, two-channel setup, and they get the job done well enough. Dialogue came through clearly, which is the most important thing for a TV like this, but big moments, like the action scenes in "Wolverine," could use more punch and low-end weight than a pair of stock budget TV speakers can provide.

The fix is the same as it is for just about every TV: get one of the best soundbars. Luckily, the eARC-enabled HDMI port makes pairing one easy, so you can upgrade your audio without much hassle.

Sources indicate that the 65M7SR runs Roku OS, and it's still the interface I'd pick over most others. The home screen is free of clutter (mostly), finding something to watch is painless, and every major streaming app is right there waiting for you. You also get support for Apple AirPlay, Apple Home, Alexa, and Google Home.

In a recent development, roku's home screen still has a fair number of ads, and you'll notice them. But compared to the busier layouts on many competing TVs, it's easy to live with. If you want minimalism in your OS, Roku remains at the top of the pack.

The 65M7SR comes with the basic Roku remote, and it does exactly what you'd want it to do. It has a voice button for hands-free searching, dedicated buttons for popular streaming services, and a layout so straightforward that you could hand it to a guest, and they'd figure it out in seconds. It also has a relatively small form factor, which is great news if you’re averse to bulky peripherals (not so great if you often lose your remote, though).

The Hisense 65M7SR is a great pick for anyone looking to step up to Mini-LED for a low price. It delivers a vivid, colorful picture, smooth, responsive gaming, and Roku's excellent interface at a price you just can't beat. The 60Hz panel, HDMI 2.0 ports, and underwhelming speakers keep it from a perfect score, but none of them ruined my time with it.

It has been revealed that if you want a faster 144Hz panel and HDMI 2.1 ports for gaming, look to the Hisense U6SF Pro, though it usually runs a couple hundred dollars more. If you're comparing it to other budget Mini-LED sets, the Hisense QD7 and Vizio VQM65C are both worth a look, too. The TCL QM64L is another good budget Mini-LED pick if you prefer Amazon’s Vega OS to Roku’s. But if you want an easy, great-looking TV that won't drain your wallet, the Hisense 65M7SR should absolutely be on your shortlist. Just do yourself a favor, and make sure you get it on sale.

#73836. Tech Report: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1167 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1167 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities.
  • Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?
  • The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

Speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s new security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

In a recent development, alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

Industry observers note that according to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”.

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target.

According to recent reports, how? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

Custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’.

It has been revealed that however, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of newly introduced software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, states cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

In a recent development, bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

As a result, we may face a new, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security complications, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

It has been revealed that also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are.

According to recent reports, penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security concerns introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance.

CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

Sources indicate that apple is exploring how people use AI for their health, presumably to build its own AI health coach. On Sunday, it released the Apple Health AI Usage Study, which could contribute to the next AI health experience Apple builds by measuring the quality of AI health responses, comprehension, and everyday health behaviors, according to a press release.

Apple is conducting the study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform widely used by healthcare professionals. The study examines the relationship between conversational AI tools, like chatbots, and the people who use them.

“Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in the press release.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for.

Sources indicate that participants are encouraged to share their HealthKit data and query the health app with questions. The study will also explore how AI tools can best prepare patients ahead of clinical visits. Apple will monitor the AI’s clarity and approachability when providing medical information, and each response or recommendation will be linked to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Responses could be unclear or incomplete, which is why Apple is rolling this out as a study to explore a responsibly designed AI health assistant.

Apple often launches studies for features it would like to develop in the future. For example, many of the hearing health features launched on the AirPods were a direct result of the findings from Apple’s Hearing Study.

Also: Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now.

Sources indicate that the AI usage study comes on the heels of the revamped Health app’s debut, which releases officially next month. It also arrives amid a bevy of AI health coaches, popping up alongside companion health devices. Google debuted its AI Health Coach in Google Health Premium last year, and Oura launched a proprietary AI model for women trained on medical standards and research from Oura’s in-house team of board-certified clinicians.

Sources indicate that A growing number of Americans are relying on AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. As AI proliferates, that percentage will only increase.

It has been revealed that “Patients and clinicians are both turning to AI, but the tools they use are being built and tested in separate worlds,” said Robert M. Wachter, M.D., UCSF’s professor and chair of the Department of Medicine, in the press release.

Apple and other tech companies are building for this latest health normal, and the AI usage study indicates that Apple isn’t taking the responsibility lightly.

Industry observers note that if you’re interested in participating in Apple’s study, it’s open to 200,000 eligible participants age 21 and older in the US. You’ll need a phone with Apple Intelligence enabled (the iPhone 15 Pro or later), running iOS 26 or later. You can download the study app to learn more and enroll.
