    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 6:50PM EST.
    • In a recent development, the expansion of artificial intelligence has pushed investors toward high-growth hardware providers.
    • Arm provides the energy-efficient architecture used in almost every smartphone, while Marvell specializes in high-speed networking and data center infrastructure.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 6:50PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Arm Holdings ›.

    In a recent development, the expansion of artificial intelligence has pushed investors toward high-growth hardware providers. Choosing between Arm Holdings (ARM -14.09%) and Marvell Technology (MRVL -11.69%) requires a careful look at their different roles in the chip ecosystem.

    Arm provides the energy-efficient architecture used in almost every smartphone, while Marvell specializes in high-speed networking and data center infrastructure. Both companies are positioned to benefit from the rising demand for accelerated computing, yet they offer distinct risk profiles and valuation levels. This comparison helps you determine which path fits your investment strategy through 2027.

    In the rapidly evolving world of semiconductor stocks, Arm is unique because it did not actually manufacture chips historically. Instead, it designs the primary architecture and licenses its intellectual property. Its energy-efficient designs are in over 99% of smartphones, although the company is now expanding into cloud data centers and automotive applications, and aims to produce its own chips at last.

    Industry observers note that the tech giant has shifted toward more complete chip designs to command higher royalty rates. This model creates a high-margin recurring revenue stream. Since it serves almost every major chipmaker, it sits at the heart of the tech sector.

    According to recent reports, in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $5.5 billion, representing growth of 23.8% compared to the prior year. This expansion is supported by the adoption of its latest v9 architecture, which carries higher royalty rates than previous generations. The company reported net income of $936.0 million during this period.

    As of its March 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.1x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity to help you understand how much a organization relies on borrowing. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with current assets, was a robust 6.0x.

    In the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, free cash flow reached $979.0 million. Free cash flow is the cash remaining after a business pays for operations and equipment. Note that stock-based compensation (SBC) represented roughly 69% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

    Marvell focuses on the infrastructure that makes modern data centers and telecommunications networks possible. The firm specializes in data processing units, networking silicon, and storage controllers. Its recent growth is driven by the need for high-speed connectivity between servers in artificial intelligence clusters.

    The organization faces significant customer concentration, as its ten largest customers represented roughly 82% of net revenue in its latest annual report. One distributor accounted for approximately 37% of sales, which adds a layer of risk to the business. Despite this, its specialized silicon is vital for major cloud service providers.

    In the 12 months ended Aug. 1, 2026, revenue reached $9.5 billion. This reflects a growth rate of 30.6% over the previous twelve-month period. During this same window, the firm generated net income of $2.6 billion, showing significant improvement from previous years.

    As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.3x, indicating a low reliance on debt. The current ratio stood at roughly 2.0x, indicating a healthy ability to meet short-term financial commitments.

    In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, free cash flow was $1.4 billion. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 33.8% of operating cash flow.

    Sources indicate that arm faces risks related to the concentration of the smartphone market. If global phone sales slow, its royalty revenue could stagnate. The organization also competes with open-source alternatives like RISC-V, which some manufacturers may prefer to avoid licensing fees. Furthermore, its heavy reliance on the licensing model means any loss of key partnerships with giants like Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) or Qualcomm (QCOM -7.45%) could impact its long-term growth prospects.

    Marvell Technology deals with significant customer concentration and geopolitical uncertainty. Trade restrictions and export controls regarding China have created supply chain challenges and impacted demand. The tech giant is also navigating a massive $115 billion all-stock acquisition of Lumentum Holdings (LITE -13.94%), which carries integration risks and potential shareholder dilution. Additionally, it recently settled patent litigation with Credo Technology Group Holding (CRDO -15.20%), highlighting the constant legal threats in the specialized silicon market.

    Marvell Technology appears more attractive on a valuation basis, offering lower Forward P/E and P/S ratio multiples than Arm.

    Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

    It has been revealed that for investors seeking exposure to the artificial intelligence boom, Arm and Marvell are two compelling stocks to own. Between the two, I would prioritize picking up shares of Marvell going into 2027.

    It has been revealed that marvell sports a much lower share price valuation than Arm, providing a greater opportunity for a superior return. Arm arguably deserves the elevated valuation multiples because of its high-margin licensing moat. However, given its foray into making its own semiconductor chips, it risks compressing those robust margins due to manufacturing costs.

    According to recent reports, marvell's stock was beaten down after it announced it was acquiring Lumentum. I think the acquisition is a smart move. Lumentum provides high-speed optical capabilities for transferring massive amounts of data, a key competitive advantage to winning AI customers. The appeal of Lumentum's solutions is illustrated by its sales of $1.3 billion for its fiscal first quarter, ended Sept. 26, which represented 137% year-over-year growth.

    Moreover, Marvell's business is exploding. It generated revenue of $8.2 billion in its 2026 fiscal year, ended Jan. 31, 2026, and the tech giant expects sales to soar to a range between $70 billion to $90 billion by its 2031 fiscal year. That growth does not include Lumentum's sales. With a lower valuation and spectacular, multi-year growth ahead, Marvell looks like the better stock to buy now.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1401 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

    College Scholarship Breakdown: Types, Sponsors and Eligibility at a Glance

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college.
    • Recent findings suggest that before you go searching for a scholarship, it's key to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding.
    • In a recent development, scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college. You can learn about scholarships in a variety of ways, but looking through an online database of available scholarships — the most common way — can be overwhelming.

    Recent findings suggest that before you go searching for a scholarship, it's key to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding. Here’s what you need to know about scholarships to decide which ones are best for you.

    In a recent development, scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies. None is better than the other when it comes to awarding funds.

    Nonprofit organizations and clubs that are looking for students either majoring in or researching certain fields, or who have experience volunteering in a specific field.

    Companies that want to support all students or only fund those majoring in a field that relates to the companies’ industries.

    Financial institutions, such as banks or credit unions, that want to support their community or their members.

    Individuals or families that are funding private scholarships, usually in memory of a loved one.

    Universities and colleges that are offering funds to students who attend their campuses.

    Research organizations that want to fund students who will research in their areas of interest and further their causes.

    Industry observers note that these scholarships generally are provided by local, state or federal government agencies for a variety of reasons. Despite being funded by a government agency, the scholarships do not require you to pay back the money — unlike federal student loans.

    Some scholarships pay for anything related to college expenses, including tuition, room and board, books and supplies, and more. Other scholarships limit what you can pay for with the funds, such as only tuition or tuition along with books. It’s key to look at this restriction when applying for scholarships to ensure the funds will go toward what you need to cover.

    Recent findings suggest that merit scholarships require you to show excellence or achievements in your schoolwork, through talents and abilities, and even leadership or service work. Because these types of awards can be highly competitive, merit scholarships might require more than just achievements, such as volunteer or leadership experience. This means merit-based scholarships can overlap with other types of scholarship categories. Here are some examples of merit-based scholarships:.

    Recent findings suggest that merit scholarships often require you to have earned a minimum grade point average (GPA). The minimum GPA depends on the scholarship but often ranges from 2.0 to 4.0, with more competitive scholarships usually requiring higher GPAs. Scholarships with lower GPA minimums are more likely to consider additional factors, such as financial need.

    Some merit scholarships might require a minimum ACT or SAT score instead of a GPA — or in addition to a minimum GPA.

    According to recent reports, merit scholarships might also require applicants to have participated in activities outside of their schoolwork. This is common for scholarships that require membership in a certain group or organization. For example, membership in agricultural clubs, such as 4-H or FFA, and scouting groups, such as the National Eagle Scout Association, appear in scholarship requirements.

    Industry observers note that some scholarships emphasize volunteering or community service and only consider applicants who have that experience. Applications vary in how detailed their requirements can be. Some scholarships want only a general description of where and how you’ve volunteered, and others might require experience with a service project that demonstrates more leadership experience or time volunteering with a certain type of organization.

    Scholarships that are awarded to students who can’t afford college are called need-based scholarships.

    According to recent reports, unmet financial need is the difference between what it will cost you to attend college and what you can afford to pay. Because calculating how much you can afford is a complicated process, many scholarships refer to your FAFSA to document your financial need.

    Recent findings suggest that some scholarship requirements may be as straightforward as demonstrating that you have financial need, but some scholarships might have income limits. However, income restrictions are less common.

    According to recent reports, athletic scholarships are for — you guessed it — athletes. They are usually offered by colleges and universities to recruit athletes onto their collegiate teams and can be competitive. Which sports have scholarships available and the scholarship amounts vary by college.

    Even though the main criterion for an athletic scholarship is being good at your sport, you’ll likely still need to show that you can keep up with your schoolwork. Most athletic scholarships require students to earn a minimum GPA or test scores to remain eligible while they’re in college.

    Recent findings suggest that some scholarships are designated for students majoring in a general field, such as science or education, but others can be for very specific areas of study. For example, a scholarship for students majoring in a natural resource field could include majors in biology, ecology, wildlife biology, conservation education, forestry, soils and hydrology. However, a stricter scholarship might state that students have to major in more specific topics, such as biochemistry or microbial ecology.

    In a recent development, scholarships are available for active and former members of the military and members of their families. In addition to federal funds available for veterans to attend college, private organizations and some universities have scholarships for veterans to offset the cost of a degree.

    Which family members can apply for funds depends on the individual scholarship. For example, some scholarships extend to children or spouses of veterans, but some go as far in a family tree as great-grandchildren.

    Sources indicate that veteran- and military-focused scholarships might require that applicants or their family members enlisted in a certain branch, served during a particular time or conflict, or meet a certain rank or status such as receiving disability. Scholarships might also require that the applicant be a wartime veteran or family member of a wartime veteran; not all veterans meet this status.

    Scholarships are also awarded to people who identify with a certain group. Common examples of identity-based scholarships include those for people who have disabilities, belong to certain ethnic or religious groups, identify as LGBTQIA+ or are first-generation students. Some identity-based scholarships require applicants to meet several criteria, such as belonging to more than one identity group.

    Outside of what would be considered standard DEI groups, there are scholarships for applicants who identify with less common groups, such as veganism, homelessness and model railroad builders.

    In a recent development, the best scholarships for you depend on your situation. For example, if you are a skilled athlete with a good academic record, going for an athletic scholarship might give you the most funding. On the other hand, if you’re going to research a topic that isn’t common, looking for scholarships that support your research topic might be your best bet because competition could be lower.

    Good tactics to figure out which scholarships are worth your time include:.

    According to recent reports, think of the skills, talents, experience and identities that are unique to you. For example, being a child of a veteran immediately qualifies you for scholarships with fewer applicants than scholarships open to everyone. Likewise, if you embrace a certain ethnicity, identify with a specific group or have experience with a type of work, you might qualify for scholarships that appreciate and recognize those attributes more than the average scholarship.

    According to recent reports, apply if you think you're eligible. Don’t apply to just a few scholarships and hope you get them. Instead, apply for as many scholarships as you can and for which you’re eligible. This increases your chances of receiving funds. Even small scholarships can make a major impact when you add several of them together.

    Understand how you can use the money. If you already have a scholarship that covers only books, applying for the same type of scholarship isn’t helpful if you don’t need the extra funds. Instead, look for scholarships that cover the costs you have remaining.

    It has been revealed that not sure where to look? Our sister site Scholarships360.org provides students with vetted scholarship opportunities. That would be a good place to start.

    Addas a preferred source on Google.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 7:15PM EST.
    • 10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›.
    • In a recent development, berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.47%)(BRKB -0.36%) isn't exactly seen as an artificial intelligence (AI) play.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 7:15PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›.

    In a recent development, berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.47%)(BRKB -0.36%) isn't exactly seen as an artificial intelligence (AI) play. But it may have more exposure to this emerging technology than you realize. In fact, the manufacturer's large utility and energy operations present opportunities for AI-related investment that are hiding in plain sight. Here's what you need to know and what Berkshire Hathaway could easily do to increase its AI bets.

    Berkshire Hathaway is usually classified as a finance business, which isn't a bad place to put it. After all, it has large insurance operations. However, the company is really a massive conglomerate, with businesses including insurance, utilities, energy, manufacturing, housing, and retail, to provide just a short list and high-level view. In Greg Abel's first annual letter as CEO, he reported that the company had 51 non-insurance operating businesses. In a previous letter, former CEO Warren Buffett said the company owned 189 operating businesses. The definition of an operating business is probably responsible for the two different numbers, but either one you pick, the number is huge.

    Greg Abel. Image source: Getty Images.

    There is a lot hiding inside Berkshire Hathaway. But, notably, it breaks out a few large businesses, including railroads, utilities, and energy. The last two are increasingly tied to the artificial intelligence industry. The tech giant's utility operations provide the electricity that powers AI. The energy business helps supply the natural gas that lets utilities, and increasingly AI companies, generate electricity.

    To be fair, Berkshire Hathaway could easily afford to buy a technology business with its cash hoard of more than $370 billion. Only technology isn't really the type of business that Berkshire Hathaway tends to buy. Former CEO Warren Buffett long focused on acquiring boring businesses that were well run and attractively priced at the time of purchase. For example, trains, utilities, and pipelines. Greg Abel's acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison Home for $8.5 billion suggests he's not going to suddenly shift directions.

    According to recent reports, it would be exciting if Berkshire Hathaway went out and bought a giant U.S. utility, such as NextEra Energy (NEE -0.41%), or a large pipeline business, such as Enterprise Products Partners (EPD -0.91%). While Greg Abel probably wouldn't target companies of that scale, the CEO could certainly afford to buy smaller players in either sector.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    In a recent development, but that's not necessary. Both the utility and midstream sectors are capital intensive. Utilities own massive power plants that take years to build and require huge sums of money. Midstream companies are no different, with their pipelines, storage, refineries, and transportation assets. It isn't unusual for a utility or midstream company to have multi-billion-dollar capital investment plans extending as far as five years into the future.

    What that means is Berkshire Hathaway could make very large capital investments within its existing operations. And that, in fact, is probably the most likely outcome. The cash on the company's balance sheet, meanwhile, means it could easily afford the required spending. Speaking to the utility and energy segment, Greg Abel noted at the start of 2026 that, "Infrastructure built for hyperscalers and data centers must be paid for by those customers and reflect the risks tied to step-changes in long-term demand." Increasingly, data center operators appear willing to do just that.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    For example, Chevron (CVX +0.91%), a longtime holding in Berkshire Hathaway's stock portfolio, has agreed to build a power plant that will use Chevron-produced natural gas to supply dedicated power to data centers. Berkshire Hathaway could do something similar with relative ease.

    Berkshire Hathaway is unlikely to start buying up AI technology businesses. That's just not what the organization does. However, if you dig into the conglomerate's operations, you see that it still has material opportunity to invest in the AI sector. And while it would be exciting if Greg Abel augmented the company's utility and energy operations through fresh acquisitions, it is far more likely that Berkshire Hathaway will simply invest in its own operations to benefit from AI growth over time. That's the opportunity that is hiding in plain sight.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:01PM EST.
    • It has been revealed that wall Street analysts can only make educated guesses, just like every other investor.
    • Industry observers note that the key theme, however, is that SpaceX will likely only be interested in data centers that already have dedicated power.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:01PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Bloom Energy ›.

    It has been revealed that wall Street analysts can only make educated guesses, just like every other investor. But they do have an advantage since they are often industry experts. This is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann's suggestion that Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX -7.69%) could buy up stalled data centers is so interesting.

    Industry observers note that the key theme, however, is that SpaceX will likely only be interested in data centers that already have dedicated power. Here's why this is so notable and what it could mean for your stock selection process as you look at companies like Bloom Energy (BE -15.30%), NextEra Energy (NEE -0.41%), and Brookfield Renewable (BEP -2.97%).

    SpaceX has a large AI data center in Memphis that it has dubbed Colossus. It is a huge asset, and it uses massive amounts of power. To ensure there is enough electricity to run the data center, SpaceX built its own dedicated natural-gas power plant. Local residents aren't happy about this, but it highlights that SpaceX is clearly aware of the power problem posed by AI data centers.

    As the backlash against AI data centers grows, access to electricity is becoming an increasingly crucial and contentious issue. Which is why Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann thinks SpaceX could end up buying data centers that have dedicated power agreements in place. However, you don't need to play this specific angle to benefit. Increasingly, AI companies are being forced to supply their own power. And there are a handful of companies that look set to benefit, including Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable.

    According to recent reports, bloom Energy makes hydrogen fuel cells. Notably, each fuel cell it sells comes along with a long-term service contract, creating an annuity-like income stream. The manufacturer's products are factory-built and can be easily deployed wherever they are needed, providing off-grid power. The company has been losing money for years but is likely to be profitable in 2026. That could be an vital inflection point for the business.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Recent findings suggest that but investors are well aware of the opportunity, pushing the stock higher by more than 1,200% over the past three years. With a lofty price-to-earnings ratio of roughly 100x, it is very clearly a well-loved stock. And yet, the opportunity to power AI data centers remains substantial, and perhaps only getting larger. If you are an aggressive growth investor, you should at least consider Bloom Energy, even if you only end up adding it to your wish list.

    According to recent reports, nextEra Energy is one of the world's largest utilities. In fact, it is looking to get even bigger, with its proposed acquisition of Dominion Energy (D -0.56%). Notably, Dominion's regulated electricity operations include one of the world's most key data center markets. The pairing will also vault NextEra into the number two spot with regard to U.S. nuclear power generation. Basically, NextEra looks like it is doubling down on electricity demand and AI at the same time.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Industry observers note that but there's an interesting twist here. NextEra is well positioned to benefit from data centers that get attached to the grid. However, it is also one of the world's largest producers of solar and wind power, a business that falls outside of the regulated framework. So it can also sell power directly to AI customers under long-term contracts. For more conservative investors, NextEra could be an attractive way to play AI's power demand, both from within and outside the regulated framework. You'll also get to collect NextEra's well-above-market 2.9% dividend yield.

    Industry observers note that for investors looking to maximize the income they generate, Brookfield Renewable and its 5.2% may be even more attractive. The partnership is focused on clean energy, but has a surprisingly diversified portfolio. For starters, it operates hydroelectric, solar, and wind power facilities. It has increasingly been investing in battery storage. And it owns half of Westinghouse, which is one of the world's largest service providers to the nuclear power industry. On top of that, it is also geographically diversified, with assets located in North America, South America, Europe, and Asia. It is a one-stop shop for investors seeking a focused clean-energy investment and for customers seeking renewable energy.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    The key here, however, is that Brookfield Renewable largely sells power under long-term contracts outside of the regulated framework. It already has large deals with AI giants Microsoft (MSFT -2.77%) and Google. Add in the goal of at least 5% annual distribution growth, and income lovers would be remiss if they didn't at least examine Brookfield Renewable and the AI opportunity ahead of it.

    If you think Stifel analyst Jonathan Siegmann is on to something, you could simply buy SpaceX. That's fine, but it isn't the only takeaway from his insight. The real story is that access to electricity is increasingly key. And you can also play that investment theme with companies like Bloom Energy, NextEra Energy, and Brookfield Renewable.

    Nokia vs. AT&T: Which Telecom Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 8:03PM EST.
    • Connectivity serves as the backbone of the modern economy, but choosing between infrastructure and services requires careful analysis.
    • Nokia focuses on the hardware and software that make networks run, while AT&T is a retail giant providing wireless and fiber service to millions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Robert Izquierdo – Updated Nov 22, 2026 at 8:03PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Nokia ›.

    Connectivity serves as the backbone of the modern economy, but choosing between infrastructure and services requires careful analysis. Investing in Nokia Oyj (NOK -8.27%) or AT&T (T +2.10%) involves balancing network equipment growth against steady subscription revenue.

    Nokia focuses on the hardware and software that make networks run, while AT&T is a retail giant providing wireless and fiber service to millions. This comparison examines their business models, balance sheets, and valuations to determine which stock is better for your portfolio.

    It has been revealed that nokia is a global connectivity infrastructure manufacturer that builds networks across fixed, mobile, IP, optical, and data center systems. The company serves communications service providers, governments, and large enterprises while operating in approximately 130 countries with roughly 78,000 employees. No single customer accounts for more than 10% of revenue, which helps diversify its revenue streams across various regions and sectors.

    Recent findings suggest that in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $22.6 billion, representing revenue growth of 4.1%. The company reported net income of $858.1 million during this period. This growth reflects ongoing investments in network technology as service providers around the world continue to upgrade their existing infrastructure.

    In a recent development, as of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 0.2x, indicating a low level of total debt relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio of 1.6x shows the organization has more than enough assets to cover its short-term liabilities. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow was $1.6 billion, which is the cash remaining after operating costs and equipment spending.

    In the 12 months ended Sept. 30, 2026, revenue reached $128.9 billion, supported by revenue growth of 3.5%. The tech giant generated net income of $13.1 billion, resulting in a net margin of 10.2%. This net margin represents the percentage of revenue that remains as profit after all expenses are paid.

    As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was 1.6x, measuring its total debt against shareholder equity. The current ratio was 0.9x. In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, free cash flow reached $19.4 billion, providing significant capital for dividends and network upgrades.

    Sources indicate that nokia must contend with intense competition from other global equipment providers in an industry with high research and development requirements. Rapid technological shifts in the 5G and upcoming 6G markets mean the organization must constantly innovate to maintain its market share. Geopolitical tensions also carry risks of influencing where the company can deploy its critical national infrastructure projects.

    Recent findings suggest that AT&T faces significant risks from increasing competition in the wireless and broadband sectors, particularly from cable providers and businesses like EchoStar (ECHO -8.72%). The company is vulnerable to supply chain disruptions and inflationary pressures on network equipment costs. It also faces potential legal liabilities from lead-clad cables and risks associated with labor union contract negotiations for 43% of its workforce.

    AT&T appears more attractively valued based on its lower earnings multiple, while Nokia offers a significantly more conservative balance sheet profile.

    Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

    Sources indicate that weighing whether to invest in Nokia or AT&T comes down to a trade-off between the former's shift toward artificial intelligence infrastructure and balance sheet cleanliness versus the latter's predictable cash flow and higher dividend income. AT&T is the better fit for conservative investors prioritizing passive income and a more attractive valuation.

    However, I would buy Nokia for 2027. While AT&T sports a robust dividend yield of about 5%, it has not raised its dividend payment since cutting the amount in 2022. It also holds a lot of debt, as evidenced by its debt-to-equity ratio of 1.6x.

    Nokia has the stronger balance sheet, and its focus on AI infrastructure is paying off. In the third quarter, AI and cloud sales soared 123% and customer orders rose 118% year over year.

    Nokia's AI radio access network (AI-RAN) technology uses artificial intelligence to intelligently manage traffic on 5G networks for better speed, coverage, and capacity. AI-RAN is still being tested but is approaching commercial deployment. Thanks to its artificial intelligence business, Nokia stock has a higher potential for share price appreciation than AT&T.

    By Daniel Sparks – Nov 22, 2026 at 8:23PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Vanguard Information Technology ETF ›.

    Sources indicate that the tech sell-off that started in October has become a correction. As I write, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC -5.28%) has dropped around 13% from its all-time closing high, hit on Oct. 6.

    The Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT -7.00%) has dropped even more. It finished at $104.99 on Nov. 19, its lowest close since May 4 and around 19% below its own Oct. 6 record of $129.80.

    That remarked, the fund's still up around 12% in 2026 as of this writing, counting dividends.

    When the fund was about 10% below its peak in late October, I didn't think it was a bargain yet. At today's price, I do.

    The businesses in it have kept growing their earnings as the share price dropped, and I'd be glad to pay the resulting valuation for a fund I strategy to hold for years to come.

    Recent findings suggest that the fund owns 315 stocks, but a handful of them drive it. As of Oct. 31, Apple was around 18% of its assets, Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) about 17%, and Microsoft about 12%.

    It has been revealed that these three haven't moved in step. Apple stock is within about 2% of its record as of this writing. Nvidia, though, has fallen about 29% since Oct. 30 alone. By my math, Nvidia by itself is behind about half of the fund's 10% fall since then.

    The slide came with a leadership change. Nvidia noted on Nov. 12 that Jensen Huang had resigned as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. On Nov. 19, California's attorney general followed with an investigative subpoena over whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information might have gone to China, and if the manufacturer misled investors about that risk.

    But Nvidia's business is still booming. In the third quarter of its fiscal 2027 (the period ending Oct. 25), the manufacturer's revenue more than doubled year over year to $115.8 billion. Data center revenue climbed 110%, and non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share surged 111%. Management also forecast fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of about $130 billion.

    In other words, much of the fund's fall has come from investors paying less for the same chip profits, not from those profits dropping.

    According to recent reports, vanguard lists the average price-to-earnings ratio of the stocks in the fund, and that number has dropped a lot in the last year and a half. The fund's holdings traded at about 39 times earnings at the end of June 2025 and about 35 times earnings on April 30, 2026. By Sept. 30, the number was about 33 times earnings, and on Oct. 31, it was 29.5 times earnings.

    Granted, that last reading came before the latest 10% slide. With earnings held flat, today's price would put the ratio closer to 26 or 27 times earnings.

    In a recent development, that's a substantial shift for a share price that is now right back where it was in late April, when it closed around $103. By my rough math, every share of the fund now carries about a third more earnings than it did then.

    The gap to the broader market has shrunk, too. On Oct. 31, the stocks in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF traded at around 24 times earnings, so the tech fund's premium had fallen to about a quarter. For businesses whose profits are still growing this fast, I think the price is fair.

    In a recent development, sure, the fund might keep sliding. A correction can become a bear market (a drop of 20% or more), and the fund is already near that mark. And with three stocks making up almost half of its assets, a tough patch for just one of them can drag on the whole fund.

    NYSEMKT · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    But a long holding period changes how much a fall like this matters. After all, this year has already shown how quickly the mood can turn.

    The fund closed at around $84 on March 30 (adjusted for its 8-for-1 stock split in April), and it then rose about 55% to its Oct. 6 high in just over six months.

    No one knows where this sell-off stops. But an investor planning to hold for five or 10 years is largely buying the earnings these companies produce in that stretch. And those earnings seem to have kept climbing through both of this year's sell-offs.

    Is the fund worth buying at around $105 a share? I think so. Its valuation has fallen far more than its price, and its largest companies are still growing. I'd buy the fund now, maybe in a few chunks over the coming months, because the sell-off might go further first.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (843 w)
    📖 Baca
    EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fool ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Forget Flying Roadsters. Tesla Investors Have 3 Bigger Challenges to Watch.

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tesla (TSLA -7.64%) knows how to get people talking and investors hyped.
    • How expensive could its legal battles become?
    • According to recent reports, none of those questions gets answered by an impressive product demonstration (the Roadster).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Daniel Miller – Nov 22, 2026 at 9:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Tesla ›.

    Tesla (TSLA -7.64%) knows how to get people talking and investors hyped. Futuristic vehicles, robotaxis, and humanoid robots give investors plenty to chew on. Those ideas are awesome, but the investment story also depends on less glamorous questions.

    Can Tesla defend its customer base? How expensive could its legal battles become? And will its next big manufacturing bet be as lucrative as investors hope?

    According to recent reports, none of those questions gets answered by an impressive product demonstration (the Roadster). Here are three challenges worth keeping on investors' radar.

    Sources indicate that tesla's domestic sales in China dropped 66.1% year over year to 8,817 vehicles in October. China's battery-electric passenger-car market declined just 5.3%, making it difficult to blame Tesla's entire slide on a struggling market.

    Industry observers note that tesla's Shanghai factory exports provided a cushion, increasing roughly 66% to 59,012 vehicles. Tesla typically emphasizes exports early in a quarter, so October alone should be taken with a grain of salt. Still, its Chinese retail sales have declined year over year for five consecutive months.

    The catch is that competitors are chasing overseas buyers, too, because China's domestic market can't seem to escape a nasty price war. BYD's (BYDDY -4.27%) overseas shipments jumped roughly 103% in October, helping counter sluggish demand and intense price competition at home.

    Recent findings suggest that exports give Tesla another outlet, but they don't give it an escape hatch from competition. The investor question is whether it can defend sales and pricing as rivals expand internationally, because Chinese autos are spreading globally, and rapidly.

    Recent findings suggest that tesla's technology promises also carry a growing legal exposure. An April Electrek analysis estimated potential financial exposure across lawsuits and regulatory matters at $2.7 billion to $14.5 billion. To be clear, that's an outside estimate of possible outcomes -- not an amount Tesla owes, has reserved, or expects to pay.

    According to recent reports, for something more concrete, consider the Benavides Autopilot case. A jury awarded $129 million in compensatory damages, assigning Tesla 33% of the fault, plus $200 million in punitive damages. Tesla's portion works out to approximately $243 million. The company is appealing, according to its latest quarterly filing.

    The legal picture isn't moving entirely against Tesla, either. Its filing also disclosed that an appeals court vacated class certification in a separate driver-assistance advertising case in October. That case returned to the lower court for further proceedings.

    Tesla notes it cannot reasonably estimate potential losses in these matters. Investors shouldn't treat the $14.5 billion estimate as an incoming invoice, but unfavorable outcomes could still produce substantial expenses or cash payments.

    Industry observers note that if there's one word Wall Street strongly dislikes, it's uncertainty. Legal uncertainty and potential costs deserve a place alongside the excitement about what Tesla's new businesses bring to the table.

    NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    Recent findings suggest that musk notes Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around mid-2027 to make room for more Cybercabs. Tesla is choosing where to put valuable manufacturing resources.

    Changing direction can be sensible, especially considering the Cybertruck failed to gain traction with consumers. Sticking with a product just because management once loved it would hardly be a winning strategy.

    On the flip side, building more Cybercabs isn't the same as building a profitable robotaxi business. Tesla needs enough paying rides to cover vehicles, charging, maintenance, insurance, and fleet operations.

    According to recent reports, further, Tesla needs to walk before it can run. There's also a compliance question. In September, federal regulators opened an investigation into Tesla's self-certification that Cybercab meets federal safety standards. To be clear, that inquiry isn't a finding of anything wrong, but it highlights another factor to consider beyond factory production.

    Factory floor space doesn't pay shareholders back on enthusiasm or hype alone. Investors need evidence that the business replacing the Cybertruck can generate attractive returns, and right now we have a lot of hype but also many questions.

    Recent findings suggest that tesla's ambitions remain compelling, and also a little daunting, if investors are honest about the company turning from a vehicle manufacturer to more of a technology conglomerate. But defending its customer base at home and abroad, managing legal exposure and regulatory hurdles, and turning robotaxis into a worthwhile business will help determine how much of that promise reaches shareholders.

    Industry observers note that enjoy the futuristic vehicles, barrel rolls, and all. Just keep an eye on the business paying to develop that wild future.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By The Motley Fool Team – Nov 22, 2026 at 9:37PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than QuinStreet ›.

    Sources indicate that on its earnings call, held on Nov. 4, 2026, for its 2027 fiscal first quarter ended Sept. 30, QuinStreet (QNST -2.73%) announced revenue grew 46% year over year to a record $416.7 million. The tech giant operates a digital performance marketing network, which matches online consumers with client products to generate measurable customer leads.

    Broadening demand across auto insurance and home services validates its media distribution model. Three things management stated on the call stand out.

    According to recent reports, automated search tools require structured data and strict compliance rules to route insurance shoppers without creating security risks or brand erosion for carriers. Management positioning its network as a control layer, or central intermediary, allows client databases to connect safely with automated shopping programs.

    It has been revealed that home services revenue surged 86% year over year to $145.7 million in the quarter, driven by contractor demand and the integration of HomeBuddy, a contractor customer acquisition business acquired in 2026. QuinStreet also expanded its contractor offerings through Get The Referral, a customer referral software platform owned by the company.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 10 stocks we like better than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ›.
    • Recent findings suggest that despite outstanding results for its latest quarter, Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) stock keeps sinking.
    • Investors like to avoid uncertainty, although no one ever knows what will happen next; the entire episode was unexpected.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    By Jennifer Saibil – Nov 22, 2026 at 10:00PM EST.

    10 stocks we like better than Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing ›.

    Recent findings suggest that despite outstanding results for its latest quarter, Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) stock keeps sinking. It's down 19% year-to-date, and it's clear that, for the time being, investors are concerned about what's coming up for the artificial intelligence (AI) powerhouse.

    Investors like to avoid uncertainty, although no one ever knows what will happen next; the entire episode was unexpected. However, some companies have tried-and-true businesses that can withstand rigorous investor scrutiny, minimizing their risk.

    If you're looking for a top AI company that fits the bill, consider Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM -9.48%).

    Recent findings suggest that investors are worried about Nvidia for several reasons right now. No one knows what Nvidia will look like without Jensen Huang at its helm, and CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress has remarked that deals that resemble "circular financing" will be toned down.

    It has been revealed that the changes in business approach could impact the manufacturer's financials, although Kress assured investors that demand is high, and she raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook from 70% to 75%. "Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing." She stated on Nvidia's 2027 third-quarter (ended Oct. 25) earnings call, "Our customers and our partners are with us... We've got this.".

    Image source: Taiwan Semiconductor.

    Many AI companies are feeling market concern, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Firm (TSMC). Nvidia is its largest client, overtaking Apple (AAPL -1.90%) in importance, and one of the main beneficiaries of TSMC's expansion to Arizona, its first U.S.-based facility. Kress noted that Nvidia's suppliers and partners are all behind it, and that it has secured the necessary memory and packaging to resume business as normal. She called out Taiwan Semi specifically, saying, "I see right now the leadership even from TSMC that was in our offices just this week, also fully engaged in helping us.".

    TSMC stock is still up 19% year-to-date, outperforming the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%), even though it's 25% off its high.

    While Nvidia and TSMC's success are to some degree tied together, TSMC had an excellent business before Nvidia, and it can maintain a strong business even if Nvidia does slow down. While Nvidia accounts for 22% of TSMC's revenue, it's been demanding capacity that could go to other players. In the third quarter, high-performance computing, which is where AI is, accounted for 68% of total revenue, up 22% from last year.

    NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

    In a recent development, the manufacturer's broad diversification is one of the features I always point out, and here is a live example of why that's critical. TSMC is a foundry that works with many partner clients globally. It makes semiconductors for all kinds of industries, which is why it can continue to grow even as tech trends and leaders change. There's no reason to panic about Nvidia's dominant position at this time, but whoever is in the lead will likely work with TSMC.

    The tech giant's new Arizona location provides greater capacity and helps it avoid tariffs. It also keeps it closer to its U.S. clients. It still has major expansion aims, including more buildings at the Arizona facility, and it has a location in Washington.

    Nvidia chips drive AI development, since the hyperscalers use its best-in-class chips. The new Vera Rubin system, which includes chips and computers, is in high demand. But TSMC plays an important role in making that happen, since it has the capacity to keep the chips coming. CEO C.C. Wei noted that there are several approaches to AI development right now, but since TSMC has "technology leadership, manufacturing excellence, global capacity expansion, and customer trust," all the players partner with it.

    Industry observers note that performance has been fantastic, fueled by AI. Sales increased 41% year over year (currency-neutral) in the third quarter, and gross margin improved by 6.9 percentage points. It was lower sequentially due to higher costs and growth investments. Management repeated that "a higher level of capital expenditures is always correlated with higher growth opportunities in the following years.".

    Industry observers note that if AI does slow down, Taiwan Semi might, too. It's not a sure thing, but even if it does happen, it isn't likely to last.

    At the current price, TSMC stock trades at a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 23, which is a fantastic deal on a growth stock that will continue to drive AI development and other technology.
